newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Hong Kong ship tests China-Taiwan shipping limits.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong ship tests China-Taiwan shipping limits.

text.p: A Hong Kong-owned container ship has made the first quasi-direct passage from China to Taiwan via Hong Kong, inching the rivals nearer the goal of direct shipping after 48 years of estrangement.
Taiwan's transport ministry said the Lien Fung arrived on February 23 at the southern port of Kaohsiung from China's southeastern special economic zone of Xiamen after transiting Hong Kong harbour.
Officials said it was the first such quasi-direct China-Taiwan passage since 1949, though they cautioned that Taipei still banned direct sailings across the Taiwan Strait.

The unprecedented crossing, widely seen as an incremental easing of the ban, was possible under a pact reached in Hong Kong in January by shipping executives from both sides with tacit approval of both governments.

"Kaohsiung port authorities have processed this ship under new rules adopted on January 22 allowing ships to transfer shipments between China and Taiwan via a third place," said Hsieh Ming-hui of Taiwan's transport ministry.
"This is consistent with the two sides' understanding reached during January negotiations in Hong Kong," said Hsieh, director of the ministry's navigation and aviation office.
It was not immediately known whether Beijing issued permits explicitly allowing the Xiamen-Kaohsiung passage via Hong Kong.
If such permission was issued, other shippers could be expected to try such crossings, analysts said.
Kaohsiung is heavily-industrialised Taiwan's main southern gateway and one of the world's busiest container ports.

Nationalist-ruled Taiwan and the communist mainland have been locked in a bitter and sometimes bloody ideological rivalry since the Republic of China government was defeated in a civil war in 1949 and fled into exile on the island.

Despite the long stalemate, an easing of unofficial ties since the late 1980s has enabled 30,000 Taiwan firms to pour more than US$20 billion into investments in the booming Chinese mainland -- fuelling intense pressure for an end to Taiwan's ban on direct shipping, air travel and communications.
China froze semi-official talks in mid-1995, but officials from both sides have encouraged the private sector to continue exploring ways to forge direct or semi-direct shipping links.
Under the January 22 pact, shipping companies from each side can apply to the other to mount such quasi-direct sailings via a "third place". Ten Taiwan shippers have made applications.
Because the "third place" is understood to be Hong Kong, the formula faces a daunting test on July 1 when the territory reverts to Chinese rule after more than 150 years as a British colony.
Officially, Taipei and Beijing remain divided on how direct shipping should work due to fundamental sovereignty issues.

Taiwan has proposed that direct sailings involve only ships flying third-country flags and that cargo from the mainland be handled at "offshore transshipment centres" elsewhere in Asia or in Taiwan but outside Taiwan customs.
All major Taiwan shippers have ships registered overseas.
Beijing, which sees Taiwan as a rebel-held part of its territory, issued rules in 1996 calling China-Taiwan shipping a domestic matter -- an approach at odds with Taiwan's plan.
One analyst said Taiwan could use Hong Kong as a transshipment centre under a broad interpretation of its rules.
"Taiwan can try to expand its interpretation of the rules to include Hong Kong as its transshipment centre," he said.
